book_title: 2. Inside the Roll: Segments, Chemistry & Real-World Economics
question: What exact products does Garware Hi-Tech Films sell, how much does each segment contribute, and what does a real-world customer transaction look like?

epigraph.quote: A great specialty film is invisible to the naked eye, yet it does the work of a structural barrier, a heat shield, and a sacrificial armor.
epigraph.author: Polymer Engineering Maxim

web_blocks.html: Garware Hi-Tech Films reports one accounting segment (Polyester Films) under Ind AS 108 [5]. In practice, management runs two divisions with very different economics. The Consumer Products Division (CPD / CPG) generated 73% of H1 FY2027 sales and 75% in Q2 FY2027 [2]. The Industrial Products Division (IPD) accounted for 27% of H1 FY2027 sales and 25% in Q2 FY2027 [2]. Value-added specialty products now represent 86% of total revenue [2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Consumer Products (SCF + PPF) drive ~75% of revenue and ~88–90% of consolidated EBITDA; Architectural films command the highest unit margins (40–45% EBITDA) and are scaling toward a ₹1,000 crore medium-term target [2].

web_blocks.title: 1. Sun Control Films (SCF) — Automotive & Architectural (51% of Q2 FY27 Revenue)

web_blocks.html: GHFL is India's sole maker of Solar Control Window Films [7, 11]. It is also one of the few global firms using patented deep-dyeing instead of surface-dipping, which stops UV color fading [7, 11]. Within SCF, Automotive Window Films block infrared heat and up to 99% of UV rays across multiple tiers [4, 7]. These include Bronze, Silver, Gold, Safety Glazing, and Sunroof films [4, 7]. In India, aftermarket automotive tints face recurring traffic-enforcement friction stemming from the Supreme Court's 2012 ban on dark films; GHFL mitigates this through IS 2553-certified safety glazing films meeting amended CMVR Rule 100 limits (70% visible light transmission front/rear, 50% side windows) (Garware CMVR Guidelines, 2025). Architectural Films are the fastest-growing line, rising from 5–10% to 30% of window film sales (~₹400 crore annual run rate) [2, 4, 5]. They serve towers, hotels, and homes with heat-rejection, anti-graffiti, 4–8 mil safety films, and PDLC privacy films [2, 7].

Concrete End-to-End Customer Example (Architectural & Home Solutions): Picture a glass office tower in Gurugram or a villa in Dubai facing 45°C summer heat. Replacing facade glass with double-glazed low-emissivity units costs crores. Instead, the owner hires a Garware Home Solutions (GHS) partner to retrofit 50,000 sq. ft. of glass with Spectra Glaze 70 film [7]. GHFL makes the deep-dyed, sputter-coated PET roll at Waluj and ships it to its regional hub. A certified crew applies the clear film inside without disrupting tenants. The building cuts cooling loads and blocks 99% of UV rays with no visible darkening. GHFL earns 40–45% EBITDA margins, plus 10–15% more via its D2C GHS studio network [2, 7].

web_blocks.title: 2. Paint Protection Films (PPF) & Detailing (24% of Q2 FY27 Revenue)

web_blocks.html: GHFL launched PPF in April 2021 and doubled output via a ₹125 crore, 300 LSF line in September 2025 (600 LSF total) [11, 13]. The division makes multi-layer thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) films with self-healing top coats [11, 13]. When gravel or swirl marks scratch the surface, heat from sunlight or warm water lets the polymer reflow and heal. Management cites ~60% share in India's branded/organized PPF segment (~3% car penetration vs. ~20% in the US and China) [2], though DGTR's June 2026 anti-dumping investigation (Case AD (OI)-15/2025) documented that low-priced Chinese TPU imports surged 13.7x to 492 MT in CY2024, leaving GHFL with less than one-quarter of total Indian domestic PPF volume and domestic PPF losses during that period. Exports to the US and Middle East therefore anchor PPF profitability [2].

Concrete End-to-End Customer Example (Automotive PPF): A buyer in Bengaluru takes delivery of a ₹75 lakh SUV and wants to guard its paint from stone chips and acid rain. The owner visits one of 250+ Garware Application Studios (GAS) [4]. A certified installer picks a 200-micron Garware Titanium PPF roll [7]. Using pre-cut patterns, the studio wraps the bumper, hood, fenders, and doors in a 6-to-8-hour wet install with Garware Application Gel [7]. The buyer gets an 8-to-10-year warranted finish. GHFL earns 20–25% EBITDA margins on the roll [2]. Management expects 150–200 bps higher margins once its Lubrizol-partnered TPU line replaces imported base film [2, 9].

web_blocks.title: 3. Industrial Products Division (IPD) (25% of Q2 FY27 Revenue)

web_blocks.html: IPD runs 42,000 MTPA of BOPET capacity and 3,600 MTPA of thermal lamination lines at Waluj and Chikalthana [11, 13]. Instead of chasing thin packaging film, GHFL targets industrial niches [7, 10]. These include high-shrink PET label films (replacing PVC sleeves), motor insulation, food lidding, and silicone release liners [7, 10]. IPD works as a crude-linked pass-through business at 10–12% EBITDA margins [2]. It absorbs fixed overhead on GHFL's 66,000 MTPA chip reactor [11] and supplies base PET film to CPD.

Concrete End-to-End Customer Example (IPD Shrink & Electrical): A European beverage bottler drops PVC shrink sleeves to meet EU recycling rules and buys GHFL's Shrink PET Film [7, 10]. GHFL extrudes the oriented PET film in Aurangabad and ships jumbo rolls to a European converter. The converter prints labels and sleeves the bottles, letting the whole bottle recycle in one PET stream. Likewise, a motor maker at CWIEME Berlin buys GHFL's thermal-resistant BOPET film to wrap stator windings [7, 9].

book_paragraphs: To make sense of Garware Hi-Tech Films, you have to stop thinking of it as a single 'plastic film' company. On paper, under Indian accounting standards, it reports one segment: Polyester Films. In reality, inside the Waluj and Chikalthana plants in Maharashtra, two completely different economic engines are running side by side—one a high-margin consumer and architectural brand, and the other a steady, crude-linked industrial supplier.

Let's walk through the three pillars that make up every ₹100 of revenue today. Roughly half of the company's top line—51% in Q2 FY2027—comes from Sun Control Films. You probably know this product as automotive window tint, where Garware holds a 60% to 65% share in India and exports heavily to North America and the Middle East. What makes Garware technically distinct is its patented deep-dyeing process: instead of dipping a finished film into a dye bath, where UV rays eventually bleach the color into an ugly purple, Garware embeds the dye and UV absorbers inside the polymer matrix itself. One domestic regulatory nuance worth keeping in mind is that Indian aftermarket car tints still face periodic state RTO enforcement friction after the Supreme Court's 2012 ban on dark films; Garware navigates this with IS 2553-certified safety glazing films compliant with amended CMVR Rule 100 visibility limits (70% front/rear, 50% sides). Over the past three years, management has taken that same solar-control science off car windows and put it onto buildings. This Architectural Films vertical has surged from 5% or 10% of window film sales to 30%—an annualized run rate of roughly ₹400 crore—and it is the single most profitable product in the entire company, earning 40% to 45% EBITDA margins.

Picture how an architectural sale works in the real world. Suppose a commercial IT park in Gurugram or a glass-clad hotel in Dubai wants to slash its air-conditioning bill without tearing out millions of dollars of facade glass. A certified Garware Home Solutions or architectural partner installs spectrally selective film on the interior glass surface. It lets natural daylight in while rejecting infrared heat and 99% of UV rays. When Garware sells that film through its own direct-to-consumer Home Solutions studios, it captures an extra 10% to 15% margin on top of its already lucrative architectural economics.

The second pillar—24% of revenue in Q2 FY2027—is Paint Protection Film, or PPF. Five years ago, Garware barely made PPF. Today, after commissioning a second ₹125 crore line at Waluj in September 2025, it has 600 lakh square feet of capacity and cites roughly 60% share of India's branded, organized PPF market. Yet our forensic check of the June 2026 DGTR anti-dumping record revealed an important qualifier: because low-priced Chinese TPU imports jumped nearly fourteenfold to 492 metric tons in calendar year 2024, Garware's share of total Indian domestic PPF volume stood below one-quarter during that period, and domestic PPF actually ran at a loss—meaning exports to the US and Middle East carry the segment's 20% to 25% EBITDA margins. If you buy a ₹70 lakh SUV in Mumbai or Dallas and take it to a Garware Application Studio, a trained technician wraps the painted body panels in a 200-micron, optically clear thermoplastic polyurethane film. When flying gravel hits the bumper, the film absorbs the impact; when parked in the sun, the elastomeric top coat literally heals minor swirl marks. Right now, PPF margins are capped because Garware still imports the raw TPU base film. That is about to change with its Lubrizol-partnered TPU extrusion plant.

The third pillar—the remaining 25% of revenue—is the Industrial Products Division, or IPD. This is the legacy 42,000-metric-ton BOPET business: recyclable PET shrink sleeves for beverage bottles, electrical insulation for motors, thermal lamination, and release liners. Margins here are a modest 10% to 12%, and raw material prices pass straight through. So why keep it? Because IPD keeps the 66,000-ton polyester chip reactor humming at high utilization, spreads fixed factory overhead, and gives the consumer division a captive, ultra-low-cost base film supply. Together, those three pillars mean 86% of Garware's revenue now sits in value-added specialty films—a complete inversion of the commodity business it used to be.

Let us walk through a concrete customer transaction in each of Garware's three revenue pillars so none of this remains abstract. Start with Paint Protection Film (24% of Q2 FY27 revenue). Picture a luxury car buyer in Dallas or Mumbai taking delivery of a new ₹1.2 crore SUV. Rather than leaving the factory clearcoat exposed to stone chips, acid rain, and highway grit, the owner drives straight to a Garware Application Studio. Over two days, certified installers wrap the hood, fenders, bumpers, and mirrors in an 8-mil aliphatic TPU film engineered with a proprietary self-healing topcoat. When a pebble strikes the hood at 100 km/h, the elastomeric TPU absorbs the impact; when parked in the sun, minor swirl marks thermally self-heal back to a gloss finish.

Now walk over to the Sun Control Film pillar (51% of Q2 FY27 revenue), and specifically its fastest-growing sub-segment: Architectural Films. Imagine a commercial REIT or hospital tower in Phoenix or Mumbai with 200,000 square feet of curtain-wall glass facing afternoon sun. Replacing single-pane or older double-glazed facades with new low-emissivity glass would cost crores and disrupt tenants for months. Instead, Garware's certified architectural partners retrofit the existing interior glass with spectrally selective nano-ceramic film—rejecting over 60% of total solar energy and 99% of UV rays while keeping visible light transmission high, cutting HVAC chiller loads by 15%–25% with a payback period under three years.

Finally, consider the Industrial Products Division (25% of revenue). A global beverage bottler running high-speed shrink-sleeve labeling lines needs oriented PETG or BOPET shrink film that hugs complex contoured bottles evenly in a steam tunnel without wrinkling or splitting at 600 bottles per minute. IPD delivers that base volume and keeps Garware's 66,000 MTPA chip reactors running at high thermal efficiency—even though its 10%–12% EBITDA margins dilute the consolidated percentage.

When you step back and look at all three segments side by side, you see a deliberate portfolio architecture. Industrial Products Division acts as the base-load anchor that keeps the 66,000 MTPA polyester chip reactors humming around the clock, absorbing fixed plant overhead even when automotive or architectural demand experiences seasonal winter dips in the Northern Hemisphere.

Meanwhile, Sun Control Films and Paint Protection Films serve as the high-margin profit engines. Every incremental rupee of revenue that shifts from a 10%-margin shrink film to a 40%-margin architectural solar film or a self-healing PPF roll drops disproportionately to operating profit—which is exactly why consolidated EBITDA margins expanded from 16% in FY23 to 28.7% in H1 FY27 without a single rupee of financial leverage.

What ties all three segments together on the factory floor is fungible coating and laminating infrastructure. At Waluj and Chikalthana, Garware can shift machine hours between automotive solar control films, architectural energy-saving films, and paint protection substrates as seasonal demand swings between Northern Hemisphere summers and commercial construction cycles—keeping asset turns high without sacrificing specialty pricing.

Notice also how each segment reinforces the others across economic cycles. Industrial films keep the base polyester lines running at high utilization; automotive Sun Control Films deliver peak summer cash flow; architectural retrofits provide multi-year commercial building contracts; and Paint Protection Films capture rising per-vehicle aftermarket spend in North America, India, and the Middle East.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice the asymmetry inside Garware's revenue mix: the 75% Consumer Products business generates roughly 90% of operating profits, while the 25% Industrial division acts as an overhead-absorbing anchor. As Architectural films (40–45% EBITDA margin) grow from ₹400 crore toward management's ₹1,000 crore ambition, consolidated margins have a structural tailwind—even without aggressive volume growth in commodity packaging.
